29.title: The first words after
29.hook: he returns and says there is no Hindu and no Muslim, and the town asks what he means
29.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's words after the river as the start of his mission, and often quote them as a teaching that all people are one before God.

segments.voice: Last week ended with three days in the river, and a man who walked out of the Bein. Your line was some come back changed. Who did you go easy on? Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THREE DAYS IN THE RIVER — SOME COME BACK CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Imagine the whole town has mourned you. They dragged the river. Your sister wept. And then, on the third morning, you walk back into Sultanpur, alive, soaking wet, with a look on your face nobody can read. People crowd around. Where were you? What happened? Are you all right? And the stories say he didn't answer. For a while he said nothing at all. He gave away what he owned and sat in silence. The town waited for an explanation. When he finally spoke, it wasn't an explanation. It was one short sentence, and it set the whole town talking. Today, the first words after.
screen: `THE TOWN HAD MOURNED HIM.` → `HE WALKS BACK IN, SILENT.` → `ONE SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence, as tradition remembers it: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. You met it back on day three, as that day's line. Now you know where it comes from. Picture where he said it. Sultanpur was a town ruled by a Muslim governor, full of Hindu merchants and Muslim officials, temples and mosques, each community with its own rules about food, prayer and who you could marry. Everyone's identity was written on them. And the storekeeper who'd just come back from the dead says: neither. What did he mean? The sources don't include a footnote, so Sikhs and scholars have heard it in several ways, and it's worth hearing each. Many Sikhs hear it this way: before God, there are no labels. Beneath the Hindu and the Muslim, there are just people, all made by the one, Ik Onkar. Others hear a challenge: nobody around him was truly living up to what their faith asked. The real Hindu, the real Muslim, was hard to find, and he was calling both back to the heart of their own paths. And many Sikhs hear a third thing too: the first sign of a new path, one that wouldn't be defined by either community. These readings don't cancel each other out, and Sikhs often hold them together. What the sentence clearly isn't is contempt. Nanak spent the rest of his life sitting with Hindus and Muslims, praying, singing, eating, arguing gently, and his closest companion on the road was a Muslim. Of course the town asked what he meant. And the town's religious judge, the qazi, decided to find out for himself. That's tomorrow.
screen: `THERE IS NO HINDU, THERE IS NO MUSLIM.` · `A TOWN WHERE LABELS WERE EVERYTHING.` · `NO LABELS, A CHALLENGE, A NEW PATH.` · `NOT CONTEMPT.` · then, large: `BENEATH THE LABELS, PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and think about the labels you put on people without meaning to: liberal, conservative, rich, poor, old, young, religious, not. Pick one you use often. Now bring to mind one real person you'd put that label on. Slowly peel it off. Who's underneath? Someone who gets tired, who loves someone, who's afraid of something. Stay with that person, without the label, for a while. The bell holds the time.
The first words after. Back from the river, Nanak says: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.
Your line: beneath the labels, people. Today, notice one label you put on someone, and set it aside for one conversation. Day twenty-nine.

30.title: Praying with the qazi
30.hook: tradition says that at prayer he told the qazi his mind had wandered home to a young horse
30.carry: where is your mind right now
30.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Guru Nanak and the qazi as a sakhi about attention in prayer, and link it with his hymns on what gives worship its meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first words after. There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Your line was beneath the labels, people. Which label did you set aside? Day thirty.
screen: `THE FIRST WORDS AFTER — BENEATH THE LABELS, PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: You're standing in a place of worship. The words are familiar, you've said them a thousand times, and your body knows exactly when to stand, when to bow. And your mind? Your mind is in the parking lot. Did I lock the car? It's in tomorrow's meeting. It's replaying an argument from last week. Anyone who has ever prayed, meditated or even tried to listen to a friend knows this. The body shows up. The mind wanders off. Five hundred years ago in Sultanpur, the story goes, a religious judge had exactly that happen to him, at exactly the wrong moment, standing next to exactly the wrong person. Today, praying with the qazi.
screen: `THE BODY KNOWS WHEN TO BOW.` → `THE MIND IS IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `SULTANPUR, AT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as the janamsakhis tell it. Word of Nanak's sentence reached the governor, Daulat Khan, and the town's qazi, the Muslim judge. They called him in. If there is no Hindu and no Muslim, they said, then come and pray with us. It was Friday. Nanak went with them to the mosque. The prayer began. The governor and the qazi bowed. And Nanak stood there, quietly, and didn't join in. Afterward the qazi was indignant. You came to pray with us, and you didn't pray. And Nanak, the story says, answered gently: who was I supposed to pray with? The governor's mind, he said, was far away in Kabul, buying horses. And the qazi's mind was at home, where a mare had just given birth, worrying that the young foal might wander off and fall into the open well in the courtyard. The story says both men were silent, because it was true. Now, it's important to hear what this story isn't. It isn't mocking Muslim prayer, or any prayer. Muslim teachers themselves have long stressed that prayer needs a present heart, humble attention; there's a word for it in Arabic, khushu. Nanak's point sits right beside theirs. Tradition connects the moment with a hymn of Nanak's, in the scripture, about what makes a true Muslim. In paraphrase: let mercy be your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest living your holy book. His challenge was never to stop praying. It was to actually be there when you do. Which is exactly why the story is so uncomfortable. Every one of us has been the qazi, standing in the right place with our mind at home by the well.
screen: `THEN COME AND PRAY WITH US.` · `THE MIND IN KABUL. THE MIND BY THE WELL.` · `NOT MOCKERY. A PRESENT HEART.` · `LET MERCY BE YOUR MOSQUE.` · then, large: `WHERE IS YOUR MIND RIGHT NOW?`

segments.voice: Let's try giving one thing your whole mind. If you pray, choose one short prayer you know, from your own tradition, and say it slowly, meaning every word. If you don't, choose one simple thing: your breath, or a single sound in the room. Each time your mind wanders off to the car, the meeting, the well, notice where it went, and gently bring it back. No scolding. Just come back. The bell holds the time.
Praying with the qazi. Nanak stands at prayer and sees that the minds beside him have wandered off to horses and a foal by the well.
Your line: where is your mind right now. Ask it three times today, in the middle of doing something, and bring your mind back to where your body is. Day thirty.

31.title: Mardana and the rebab
31.hook: a Muslim musician, Bhai Mardana, becomes his lifelong companion; Mardana plays and Nanak sings
31.howItsDone: Sikh hymns are sung, not only read: in gurdwaras, musicians called ragis sing the scripture to instruments in the ragas it is arranged by, and Bhai Mardana is remembered as the first musician of the Sikh tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying with the qazi, and a mind that had wandered home to a young horse. Your line was where is your mind right now. Where was yours, the last time you tried to give something your whole attention? Day thirty-one.

Think of the best duos you know. Two friends who finish each other's jokes. A singer and the guitarist who has played behind her for thirty years. One of them is the name on the poster, and the other one is the reason the song works. Guru Nanak had one of those. His name was Mardana. He came from Nanak's own village, Talwandi, and tradition says he was about ten years older. He was a Muslim, from a family of hereditary musicians, the kind of family that played at weddings and sang the genealogies of the village. And he carried an instrument everywhere he went. When Nanak came out of the river with something to say, Mardana is the one who gave it a tune. Today, the instrument.
screen: `EVERY GREAT SONG HAS TWO PEOPLE.` → `A MUSLIM MUSICIAN FROM TALWANDI.` → `HE CARRIED AN INSTRUMENT.`

segments.voice: The instrument was a rebab: a plucked string instrument with a wooden body, skin stretched across the front, and a deep, woody voice. It's the ancestor, or at least a cousin, of instruments played across Central and South Asia today. Picture how the two of them worked. Nanak would feel a hymn coming. Tradition says he would turn to his friend and say something like: Mardana, play the rebab, the Word is coming. And Mardana would find the note, and Nanak would sing. So from the very beginning, Sikh scripture wasn't something written down and read silently. It was sung. It was born as music. That's why the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga, by musical mode, and why, in a gurdwara today, the hymns are still sung to instruments. Now notice who is holding that rebab. A Muslim musician sat at the side of a teacher born into a Hindu family, and for decades they walked together, ate together and slept on the same roads. Remember the line from a few days ago: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Mardana is that line with a face and a pair of hands. Sikhs still honor him by name. A few verses in the scripture carry his name, and his descendants, called rababis, sang the hymns in Sikh gatherings for generations. And there's one more thing in the pairing worth keeping. Neither of them did it alone. The words needed the music, and the music needed the words. With this, the early years close: the boy at Talwandi, the river, the storehouse, the first words after. Tomorrow the two of them walk out of town.
screen: `THE REBAB — STRINGS, SKIN, WOOD.` · `MARDANA, PLAY. THE WORD IS COMING.` · `SCRIPTURE BORN AS MUSIC.` · `A MUSLIM MUSICIAN AT NANAK'S SIDE.` · then, large: `ONE PLAYS, ONE SINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one piece of music, all the way through. Any music. Pick something now, or let the bell's two minutes be the music. Don't do anything else while it plays. Don't check the time. When the song gets to the part you usually skip, stay. Notice the instrument underneath the voice, the one you normally don't hear. Somebody is playing it, so the singer can sing. The bell holds the time.
Rebab. The stringed instrument Bhai Mardana played beside Guru Nanak, so the hymns could be sung. Today's word.
Your line: one plays, one sings. Today, notice someone who makes your work possible from the side of the stage, and tell them so. Day thirty-one.

32.title: Setting out
32.hook: Nanak leaves home for years of travel on foot, with Mardana beside him
32.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's udasis through the sakhis, short stories of each stop, told at home, in gurdwaras and in children's classes; many gurdwaras across South Asia stand at places tradition links to his travels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rebab, and Mardana playing so Nanak could sing. Your line was one plays, one sings. Who did you notice working at the side of the stage? Day thirty-two.

Most of us have a map of the world that's mostly a map of our own neighborhood. The grocery store, the office, a few friends' houses, the route between them. We could draw it with our eyes shut. Guru Nanak had a good job in Sultanpur, a wife, two young sons, a sister nearby who loved him. And then, some time after the river, he left it all and started walking. Not for a weekend. For years. On foot, with Mardana and the rebab beside him, sleeping where they were offered a floor and eating what they were given. From here the story changes shape. It stops being one village and becomes a road. Today, the word for that road.
screen: `A JOB, A FAMILY, A TOWN.` → `THEN HE STARTED WALKING.` → `FOR YEARS, ON FOOT.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call these journeys the udasis. Tradition counts four great ones, sometimes five, spread over something like twenty years. One went east, toward Bengal and Assam. One went south, as far as Sri Lanka, tradition says. One north, into the Himalayas. One west, as far as Mecca and Baghdad. Nobody has a travel log. What we have are the janamsakhis, life stories written down generations later, and they don't always agree on the order or the route. So the dates and the map are tradition, and Sikh historians still argue over them. Now the word itself. Udasi comes from a word that can mean detachment, even sadness, the feeling of someone who has stepped back from the world. In Nanak's time it could describe a renunciate, a wandering holy man who gave up home for good. Here's the surprise. Nanak walked like a renunciate, but he didn't preach renunciation. He came home between journeys. He never told people to abandon their families. His travels were for going out to people, not away from them. He went to the pilgrimage towns, the Muslim shrines, the mountain hermitages and the markets, and he talked with whoever was there: priests, Sufis, yogis, carpenters, thieves. And almost every stop becomes a story, a short, sharp scene that Sikh children grow up hearing. Over the next week or so we'll take them one at a time, as shorts. Think of today as the day the car pulls out of the driveway. Everything he'd said at home, there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim, he now takes out on the road, to see if it holds up.
screen: `FOUR JOURNEYS, TRADITION SAYS.` · `THE MAP IS TRADITION, NOT A LOG.` · `UDASI — STEPPING BACK.` · `NOT AWAY FROM PEOPLE. OUT TO THEM.` · then, large: `GO AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk somewhere new today. It doesn't have to be far. A street you've never turned down. The other staircase at work. The far end of the park. For now, settle and plan it. Picture the door you'll walk out of. Picture the turn you don't usually take. Then, when you get there, look the way a traveler looks, as if you might have to describe it to someone back home. The bell holds the time.
Udasi. The name for Guru Nanak's long journeys on foot, from a word for detachment, stepping back. Today's word.
Your line: go and see. Today, take the new route, and talk to one person there you wouldn't normally talk to. Day thirty-two.

33.title: Bhai Lalo's bread
33.hook: at Saidpur he eats the coarse bread of Lalo the carpenter and turns down the rich Malik Bhago's feast
33.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, as one of the three pillars of daily life alongside remembering God's name and sharing; the story of Bhai Lalo is one of the best known sakhis told to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the udasi: Nanak and Mardana walking out of town for years. Your line was go and see. Where did the new route take you? Day thirty-three.

Imagine two invitations arrive on the same night. One is from the richest man in town. There'll be a long table, silver dishes, the important people of the district, and it would do your reputation a lot of good to be seen there. The other is from a carpenter who lives in a small house at the edge of town. He's offering what he has: a few pieces of coarse, heavy bread. Guru Nanak got both invitations, tradition says, in a town called Saidpur, in the Punjab. The rich man was an official named Malik Bhago. The carpenter was named Lalo. And the whole town was watching to see which door the holy man would walk through. Today, the bread he chose.
screen: `TWO INVITATIONS, ONE NIGHT.` → `A RICH OFFICIAL'S FEAST.` → `A CARPENTER'S COARSE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Nanak went to Lalo's. He stayed with the carpenter, sat on his floor and ate his bread, which tradition describes as rough, made from coarse grain. Malik Bhago was offended. He'd laid on a feast for this visitor, and the visitor had gone to a laborer's hut instead. So he sent for Nanak and demanded to know why. The answer, in the way Sikhs tell it, was simple: Lalo's bread is earned by honest work, with his own hands. Your feast, the Guru said, was paid for by squeezing the poor. Tomorrow we'll see the famous, strange thing tradition says happened next. Today, stay with the choice. Here's why it matters so much on this path. Sikhs describe their way of life with three short commitments. Remember God's name. Share what you have. And earn an honest living, which in Punjabi is kirat. Lalo is kirat with sawdust on his hands. He isn't a priest. He isn't rich. He works, he earns, and he shares what he earns with a stranger at his door, and the Guru treats that coarse bread as the finest food in town. It's not just a story. Lalo shows up in the scripture itself. In one of Guru Nanak's hymns, in raga Tilang, the Guru speaks to him by name, O Lalo, as if talking to a friend. So a carpenter from a small town has his name in the Sikh holy book. Sikhs sometimes say it this way: the bread isn't sweet because of what's in it. It's sweet because of how it was earned.
screen: `HE WENT TO THE CARPENTER'S HOUSE.` · `THE FEAST WAS PAID FOR BY THE POOR.` · `KIRAT — AN HONEST LIVING.` · `LALO'S NAME IS IN THE SCRIPTURE.` · then, large: `HONEST BREAD IS SWEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one plain meal gratefully. Maybe it's the next thing you eat, a slice of toast, a bowl of rice. For now, settle and bring it to mind, or hold it if it's in front of you. Think about whose hands it passed through: the farmer, the driver, the person at the register, maybe you. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own way. If you don't, just let the plainness be enough. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Lalo's bread. The coarse bread of a carpenter, honestly earned, which Guru Nanak chose over a rich man's feast. Today's word.
Your line: honest bread is sweet. Today, when you eat, notice one thing that was earned by honest work, yours or someone else's. Day thirty-three.

34.title: Milk and blood
34.hook: tradition says he squeezed Lalo's bread and milk ran out, and from Bhago's feast, blood
34.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the milk-and-blood sakhi as a teaching about honest earnings; many gurdwaras and families use it to explain why kirat, honest work, matters, and some Sikhs give a tenth of their income, dasvandh, from earnings made honestly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Lalo's bread, and a feast turned down. Your line was honest bread is sweet. What did you eat that someone honestly earned? Day thirty-four.

We left the story in a tense room. Malik Bhago, the rich official of Saidpur, has summoned Guru Nanak to explain himself. Why did you eat a carpenter's coarse bread and snub my feast? The townspeople have crowded in. Everyone wants to see what happens when a holy man with nothing insults a man with everything. And this is where the story, as tradition tells it, stops being a dinner-party drama and becomes something stranger. Nanak asks for two things to be brought: a piece of Lalo's bread, and a piece of food from Bhago's table. He takes one in each hand. Today, what happened when he squeezed.
screen: `A TENSE ROOM IN SAIDPUR.` → `ONE PIECE FROM EACH TABLE.` → `ONE IN EACH HAND.`

segments.voice: Tradition says he pressed them. From Lalo's bread, milk ran out. From Bhago's rich food, blood. That's the whole scene, and it's told in gurdwaras and in children's books and painted on walls. Sikhs read it in more than one way. Many take it as a miracle that really happened, a sign given to a proud man. Others read it as a picture, a parable in the language of the janamsakhis, which are full of wonders. And it's worth saying plainly: the milk and the blood don't appear in the scripture itself. They come from the later life stories. What the scripture does have is the idea underneath, in Guru Nanak's own words. In one hymn, he says that taking what rightfully belongs to another is as forbidden as pork is to a Muslim and beef is to a Hindu. Notice how he says it. He reaches for the one thing each of his neighbors would never eat, and says: that's what stolen wealth is. So in either reading, miracle or picture, the point is the same. Food carries its history. Lalo's bread came from sweat, and it's nourishing, like milk. Bhago's feast came from taxes and bribes and squeezing people who had little, and so, in the story's startling picture, it's made of their blood. Nobody could see it on the plate. The story makes it visible. And it asks a question that doesn't expire: not how much do you have, or how nice is it, but how was it earned? Tradition says Bhago was shaken, and changed his ways.
screen: `FROM LALO'S BREAD, MILK.` · `FROM BHAGO'S FEAST, BLOOD.` · `MIRACLE OR PARABLE: SIKHS READ BOTH.` · `FOOD CARRIES ITS HISTORY.` · then, large: `HOW WAS IT EARNED?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think where one thing you own came from. Settle. Pick something near you: your shoes, your phone, the chair. Now trace it back as far as you can. Who made it? Where? Who carried it? Who was paid, and who maybe wasn't? You won't know all of it. That's fine. Just follow it as far as you can, without guilt and without a verdict. The bell holds the time.
Milk and blood. Tradition's picture of honest bread and stolen wealth, pressed in Guru Nanak's hands. Today's word.
Your line: how was it earned. Today, ask it once about something you're about to buy, and once about something you're about to earn. Day thirty-four.

fork.setup: you're Malik Bhago. the Guru has just pressed your fine food and blood has run out of it, in front of the whole town. what do you do?
options: throw him out of Saidpur.
laugh it off as a trick.
take it to heart and change your ways.
fork.reveal: tradition says Bhago was shaken and changed. the story isn't about ruining him; it's about letting him see.

original.note: Gurmukhi: hakk, what rightfully belongs to someone, from Arabic haqq; the word in Nanak's line about another's due.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick with bread.
what it means: food carries its history. honest bread nourishes like milk; wealth squeezed from the poor is, in the story's picture, their blood.
what a scholar hears: a janamsakhi wonder, not in the scripture, built on a real hymn that likens taking another's due to pork for a Muslim and beef for a Hindu.

35.title: Sajjan's rest house
35.hook: a man who robbed the travelers who slept in his inn hears Nanak sing and gives it all up
35.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Sajjan as a sakhi about transformation through the Guru's word, and the Suhi hymn linked to it is sung in kirtan; tradition places the inn near Tulamba, in present-day Pakistan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, milk and blood, pressed from a carpenter's bread and a rich man's feast. Your line was how was it earned. Did you trace one thing back? Day thirty-five, the end of a week.

Picture a rest stop on a long road. Clean, welcoming, run by a man so pleasant that his name, Sajjan, means friend, or good man. He built a place for Hindu travelers to pray and a place for Muslim travelers to pray. He offered a warm meal and a bed. And at night, tradition says, he robbed his guests, killed some of them, and threw their bodies down a well. One evening two new travelers arrived: a man with a calm face and his friend with a rebab. Sajjan looked at their clothes and their bearing and guessed they were carrying something worth taking. He showed them to their room. Today, what happened that night.
screen: `A FRIENDLY INN ON A LONG ROAD.` → `AT NIGHT, THE HOST ROBBED HIS GUESTS.` → `TWO NEW TRAVELERS ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Sajjan waited for them to fall asleep. But Nanak didn't sleep. He asked Mardana to play, and he began to sing. The hymn Sikhs link to this night is in the scripture, in raga Suhi, and it's about bronze. Bronze, the Guru sings, is bright and shiny, but rub it and the black comes off on your fingers. Wash it a hundred times and it won't wash clean. Then the images keep coming: tall buildings, painted and grand, that are hollow inside. Cranes in white feathers standing in holy water, looking for fish to kill. Sajjan stood outside the door and listened, and heard himself. The shiny front. The guest rooms for both faiths. The well. Tradition says he fell at the Guru's feet, confessed everything, and gave back what he'd stolen. The inn became a place where travelers were actually safe. It's often remembered as one of the first places where the Guru's followers gathered on the road. Here's what's remarkable. Nanak doesn't call the guards. He doesn't expose Sajjan to the town. He sings, and lets the man find the truth himself. And look back at the week. The first words after the river. The qazi at prayer, with his mind wandering off to a young horse. Mardana and the rebab. Setting out on the road. Lalo and Bhago. Milk and blood. And now Sajjan. Again and again the same pattern: an outside that looks one way, an inside that's another, and a Guru who gently shows the difference. Sikhs love this story for its last turn. If even Sajjan turned, nobody is past turning.
screen: `NANAK SANG INSTEAD OF SLEEPING.` · `BRONZE SHINES, BUT RUB IT: BLACK.` · `SAJJAN HEARD HIMSELF, AND TURNED.` · `THE WEEK: OUTSIDE VERSUS INSIDE.` · then, large: `NOBODY IS PAST TURNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing you'd like to put down. Settle, and breathe. Not your worst secret. Just one habit, or grudge, or small shiny front you keep up that you're tired of carrying. Name it to yourself, plainly. Then imagine setting it on the floor, the way Sajjan set down his loot. You don't have to do anything else with it yet. Just let your hands be empty for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Sajjan's rest house. An inn whose friendly host robbed his guests, until he heard the Guru sing about shining bronze and turned. Today's word.
Your line: even sajjan turned. Today, when you're tempted to write someone off, remember the rest house. Day thirty-five.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sajjan, a friend, a good person; the story turns on a name that didn't fit, until it did.
